newsitem.title: EGYPT: Libya says sanctions cost $19 billion.
newsitem.headline: Libya says sanctions cost $19 billion.

text.p: Libya said on Saturday that U.N. sanctions cost the country $19 billion and up to about 21,000 human lives in the first three and a half years.

A report to the Arab League by the Libyan Secretariat for Foreign Liaison and International Cooperation (foreign ministry) said most of the dead were patients who needed urgent medical treatment abroad.

The United Nations banned flights in and out of Libya from April 1992 because Libya refused to hand over for trial two Libyan men accused of blowing up a Pan Am airliner over the Scottish town of Lockerbie in December 1988.
On Saturday the Cairo office of the official Libyan news agency JANA released a resume of the Libyan report, which covers the period up to the end of 1995.

"The blockade made it impossible to send abroad about 16,000 urgent chronic medical cases which it was difficult to treat in local hospitals and health centres... This led to the death of most of these cases in tragic and cruel conditions," it said.
Seven hundred and eighty other patients were killed while travelling abroad, most of them in traffic accidents, it added.

Road accidents killed another 2,560 travellers who would normally have flown abroad and 1,135 children and 514 women had died in childbirth because of shortages of medicines that used to reach Libya by air, it said.

A breakdown of the economic costs showed that agriculture was the sector hardest hit, with losses of $5.9 billion because the country could not export its surplus of fruit and vegetables. Before sanctions, agricultural exports were tiny.
It said the sanctions had made many factories idle and put many foreign and Libyan workers out of their jobs.
The energy sector had lost about $3 billion, partly through delays in developing refineries and petrochemical projects.
